prompt:
You use the Hoare partition from the lesson, which returns a split boundary: every key through that boundary is no larger than the pivot, and every later key is no smaller. What recursive calls are correct?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.explanation: This is Lomuto's recursion, which assumes the pivot is fixed at p. Hoare doesn't put the pivot at p, so a[p] may be unsorted and is wrongly excluded.
Including p in both halves can cause infinite recursion when a sub-array doesn't shrink.
That ignores the partition completely and degrades into an O(n²) scheme (and isn't even correct).
Correct. Hoare only guarantees that the left part is no bigger than the pivot and the right part no smaller, around the split at j, so both sides including a[p] must be sorted.

workedExample:
Recall the lesson's trace on `[7, 2, 1, 6, 8, 5, 3, 4]` with pivot 6:

```
after: [4,2,1,3,5,8,6,7], j = 4
left  a[0..4] = [4,2,1,3,5]
right a[5..7] = [8,6,7]
```

The pivot 6 ended up at index 6, not at boundary index four. The key five at index four still needs sorting with the left part. So recurse on `[lo, p]` and `[p+1, hi]`.

Using `p - 1` would leave 5 out of the left recursion and could produce unsorted output.

prompt:
Which statements comparing the Lomuto and Hoare partition schemes are true? Select all that apply.

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Lomuto leaves the pivot at its final sorted index
options.explanation: Correct. Its last step swaps the pivot into position i, between the smaller and larger elements.

options.text: Hoare needs roughly one third of Lomuto’s expected swaps on uniformly random distinct keys
options.explanation: Correct under that input model. Hoare swaps pairs misplaced on opposite sides; Lomuto swaps each smaller key it meets. This is not a bound for every input.

options.text: Hoare also leaves the pivot at its final sorted index
options.explanation: No. Hoare only guarantees that everything in a[lo..j] is no bigger than the pivot and everything in a[j+1..hi] no smaller; the pivot can end up anywhere, which is why recursion uses [lo, p].

options.text: Lomuto with a strict `<` test is Θ(n²) on an array of all-equal keys
options.explanation: Correct. No element is less than the pivot, so every split of an m-element sub-array is zero versus every other key, giving a quadratic triangle of comparisons for n elements.

options.text: With Hoare's scheme, `a[hi]` is always a safe pivot choice
options.explanation: No. If a[hi] is the unique maximum, j comes back as hi, the left range [lo, hi] doesn't shrink, and recursion never ends. Use a middle (or lower) element.

workedExample:
Compare on `[7, 2, 1, 6, 8, 5, 3, 4]` (from the lesson):

| | Lomuto (pivot 4) | Hoare (pivot 6) |
|---|---|---|
| Swaps | 3 + final | 3 |
| Pivot final? | Yes, index 3 | No (ends at 6, boundary index four) |
| Recurse on | [lo,p−1], [p+1,hi] | [lo,p], [p+1,hi] |

On all-equal input, Lomuto's `<` sends everything to one side (quadratic), while Hoare's pointers stop on equal keys and meet in the middle (balanced).
